en: The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Changling Zhuo of Tiantong Wannian Wanshou Chan Monastery in Tokyo,
Compiled by His Dharma Heir Jiechen, while he was Abbot of Xianing Yongbao Chan Monastery in Wulin.

When the Master first resided at the Gānlù Chan Monastery in Shū Prefecture, on the day he ascended the hall, after offering incense to pray for the longevity of the Emperor, he again held up some incense and said:

"This single portion of incense has no great scent, yet it can penetrate upward through the cranial gates of the Buddhas of the three periods and reach downward to the wondrous source of all sentient beings. Even if the various demons wish to hide..."

It is exposed. Though the thousand eyes have no means to see it, today I bring it forth; yet it has already fallen into the realm of conventional ritual. Since there is this auspicious connection, it cannot fail to be proclaimed.
I burn incense in the burner as an offering to Master Lingyuan of the Zhaomo Hall on Huanglong Mountain in Hongzhou, to repay the milk of the Dharma.
Thereupon, he ascends the seat. After the head monk has struck the gavel, a monk asks: "The Heart-Seal of Central India—"
Transmitted from a source deep within, this secret treasury of the *maṇi* jewel is brought forth before the Terrace of Nectar to open the hall for the sake of the nation.
I pray that you will hear the essentials of the Dharma. The Master said: "One person may transmit what is false, but ten thousand people transmit what is real. The student stepped forward and said:

"May we long take the sun and moon as our celestial eyes, and together point to the mountains and rivers as the foundation of our longevity. The Master said: "Once the rain has moistened the earth to its full extent, the hearts of the four classes of people are already [at peace]."
Su-seng asked, "When Baoshou opened the hall for formal teaching, Sansheng pushed forward a monk. What was the underlying meaning?
The Master said, "Rarely does one encounter a guest with pierced ears; often one meets a man who marks the boat.
[The monk] further asked, "Why did he blind the eyes of the entire city of Zhenzhou? The Master said, "Advancing is not as good as retreating."
The Master spoke again: "Where there is a question and an answer, it must be the right person. If it is indeed that person, this is called the Samādhi of Playful Manifestation;

responding to the occasion as it arises, there is neither 'right' nor 'wrong. However, if the source of the mind is still obscured and the illuminating awareness remains clouded, to merely indulge wild faculties is entirely improper.
Regarding this matter, before the assembly of devas and humans has even gathered, one is already moving within the ordinary."
In the midst of stillness, within the very portion of every person, all is fundamentally and naturally blended; there is no increase or decrease for any.

As light comes and darkness goes, from antiquity to the present, this single segment of numinous light is inherently brilliant and penetrating. It is "the mind itself is the Buddha," manifest and majestic in daily life;

yet it is "neither Buddha nor mind," as each and every thing is directly perceived in its true essence. This is a subtle and wondrous gate of great liberation. To gain entry here, one transcends [all conceptualization].

Speech issues forth with its resonance reaching the ten directions; without moving, the body wanders through the sands of worlds. In every atom lies the realm of the Flower Treasury (*kusumagarbha*); in every place is the gate of *dhāraṇī*.
By means of thought and recollection, one accords with the divine mechanism; by opening the gates of worldly toil (*kleśa*), one gives rise to Buddha-works.

The stone horse turns back its path; the lotus blooms within the fire. Thus, realization is attained at the tip of the staff, the mind is transmitted beneath a shout, the source is clarified with a single finger, and the three...
Having attained the marrow through prostration, what more is there to wonder at? Can you still believe it? [The Master] strikes the meditation seat with his whisk and says:
"If you can believe here, where else would all these complications go? After a long pause, he says:
"Attaining the essential meaning before one's eyes turns everything into mere views; being without mind wherever one touches is reaching the ultimate end."
Ascending the hall, he said: "In recent years, I have newly settled at Ganlu. Being dull-witted and slow, I have nothing to do.
Yet I am forcibly assigned by the officials; my karmic conditions cannot be avoided. I can only go with the current and follow the waves, allowing it to circulate throughout all quarters.
At my gate, I buy fresh salt; in my jar, there is some aged vinegar. To those who come seeking tea, I give them tea—it is truly like this."
From poverty to wealth. He further asked about the Patriarch’s coming from the West. "Old man," [the Master] said, "if you wish to stay, then stay. Entering the hall, he said:
"The realms of boundless lands are not separated by so much as a hair’s tip from self and other. The ancients spoke only of 'the cypress tree in the courtyard.
There have always been those who have realized this matter. Ten ages of past and present—beginning and end do not depart from the present moment."
Be mindful; then go on like this. Who would dare degrade the noble to the lowly? O virtuous ones, why have you long buried the *maṇi* jewel in a dark room?

Furthermore, you must not mistakenly identify the five colors as the *maṇi*, thereby failing to distinguish between the black and the white, and remaining unable to shed the dust of emotional attachments.
Thus we know that as long as water has not entered the sea, it cannot have a salty taste; as long as gold has not been separated from the sand, it cannot be pure.
This merely results in confusion. Now tell me: where is the mani-jewel right now? After a long silence, he said:

"Go to the hall and drink tea. Ascending the hall, he said: "The scenery of the four quarters is vast and still; the empty sky stretches out before the eyes, wide and open. Who can distinguish beauty from ugliness?"

No. Why employ the conceptual mind to speculate? Like a spark of flint flashing forth, like a solitary eagle in the clear autumn sky—before the words, the essential meaning has already been fully revealed;
after the phrase, there is no trace left, nothing but vain searching. If you try to grasp it, you cannot move forward; it is like the carriage-ruts of the Qin era.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Long rains have not ceased, yet today it is clear. To blend mud with water, one must be discerning.

What harm is there if empty space becomes damp? As before, the sun rises from the eastern side. One may say that the dripping at the eaves is nothing other than the gate of perfect penetration and vastness;
that the autumnal rites are performed in spring is entirely the pure realm of Vairocana. Seen by the eye and heard by the ear..."
[The Master] said, "I have heard that losing one's money brings misfortune. You all—have you yet been able to utter the 'phrase for hiding the body'?
After a long silence, he said, "To yield to others is not the mark of a weak man."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "The realms of boundless lands are not separated from one another by so much as a hair's breadth;
why then do you say, 'Those within the hermitage do not see what is outside the hermitage'? The Master said: "Ask from within the hermitage, or ask from outside the hermitage.
The monk stepped forward and said: "Today I have encountered a great opportunity despite my small departure. The Master said: "The assembly will laugh at you. A monk asked: "What is the Dharma King?"
[The Master] seals [the question]. The Master says, "East, west, south, north. The student advances and says, "I, this disciple, do not yet understand; I pray for the definitive point.

The Master says, "Just wait and see when the command is executed. Question: When rushing currents pass through a blade and swift flames overtake the wind, what kind of skillful means (hastapāda) should one possess?
The Master said, "A note. The student asked, "In that case, advancing is not as good as retreating. The Master said, "Those closest to the fire burn first. A question was asked:
"When Danxia burned the wooden Buddha, why did the temple steward’s eyebrows and beard fall out? The Master said, "A calico cat climbing a tree.
The student said, "Had I known it would be so, it would have been better not to be so. The Master said, "Save your eyebrows."
Question: “Deishan would strike a student as soon as they entered the gate; Linji would shout as soon as they entered the gate. I wonder, Master, how do you guide people? The Master said:
“The official administration does not permit even a needle. The questioner pressed further: “Is there no expedient means? The Master said: “In private, one may pass even carriages and horses.”
Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: A monk asked Zen Master Chonghui, "Before Bodhidharma came to this land, was there still the Buddha-dharma?
Hui said, "Setting aside for a moment whether it existed before his arrival, what is the matter now? The monk said, "I do not understand.
Hui said, "Ten thousand ages of eternal sky; one morning’s wind and moon. After a long silence, he spoke again: "Do you understand? This is a matter concerning your own self."
What does it matter whether he comes or not? When he comes, he is much like a fortune-teller.
Seeing that you do not understand, he pierces through the omens for you; as soon as good or bad fortune arises, it rests upon your own part—observe everything for yourself.
The monk asked again, "What is it like to be one who understands divination? Huìyuán said, "As soon as one steps out the door, it is already inauspicious.

The Master said, "Chan Master Chōnghuì was like a bell on its stand: when struck, it rings. While this is indeed excellent, when it comes to casting the divination, he was still unable to reach a definitive conclusion.
As for the time before he had even stepped out the door—was it then auspicious or inauspicious? [Consider this], O assembly!"
"Sun Bin has opened his shop. You people have lost your sheep on many paths; for a whole night you have searched east and west but found it not.
Why do you not come out and seek a divination? After a long while, he said, "If there were no Sun Bin, I would go to seek my own divination."
He threw down his whisk and said: "The barefoot man chases the rabbit; the boot-wearing man eats the meat. He ascended the hall and said:
"At sunrise in the hour of the Rabbit, there is a great clamor and bustle. Within this, one must be skillful. Do you understand?
To make flour, one must use the wheat of that specific region; to sing the song, one must be a person from the imperial capital."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Clearly there is no coming or going; Evidently there is the old and the new. The events of this day last year— The person of this day is the person of last year.
In his entire being, he gathers and releases at will; He flows with the current, blending host and guest. The spring light leaks forth once more;
Though one has a mouth, there is no need to speak."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Step by step ascending to heights; letting go from the void. North, south, east, and west—there has never been a seam or crack.
This is the separate transmission outside the teachings; it is the ultimate mastery over all discourse."
Ascending the hall, he said: "All sentient beings, within the state of non-arising, falsely perceive arising and ceasing;
for this reason, it is called 'revolving in birth and death. The path of ambrosia: the Śrāvakas sever the obstacle of afflictions and realize the principle of the emptiness of persons;

for this reason, it is called 'the ground of tranquil extinction. The Bodhisattvas comprehend the non-self of phenomena and give rise to great compassion; for this reason, it is called 'awakening to existence.'"

"Sentimentality" refers to those of the patched-robed monastic community: when hungry, they eat; when weary, they sleep. But tell me, what kind of eyes should they possess? Entering the hall, he said:
"Wind is not something separate from coolness; fire is inherently hot. Sitting cold for nine years—originally, one has never even glimpsed it."
Ascending the hall, he said: "To level the high and accommodate the low is to invite a thief to ruin one's house; to cut through iron and sever nails is for the fox to linger in its den.
If it is none of these, then what should be done? Therefore it is said: 'Only a man of true caliber can let go completely at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff.
But as for the single phrase regarding holding the almsbowl in the Land of Fragrant Accumulation—how do you speak it? After a long silence, he said: "Be careful not to [fall into conceptualization]."
The wind blows in a different tune.
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said, "O assembly! If I hold it up, I want you all to seek a place to emerge within the gate of Samantabhadra.
He then set it down and said, "If I set it down, I teach you all..."
Turn toward the gate of Mañjuśrī and seek a path for entry.

Even if you neither grasp nor let go, it will cause all of you to abide within the realm of Vairocana, neither exiting nor entering, attaining great mastery. Although this is so, it is not yet a true heart.
How could it compare to you all ceasing your former wandering, recognizing the ancestral deed-deed, and inheriting [the lineage]?

Recognizing one’s own ancestral estate: let it follow the teaching that a pillar conceives and an iron ox gives birth to a calf. The latter four and the former three are entirely without a nest or lair.
What follows is a long discourse; with a shout and a "tut," he plants his staff upright and descends from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The golden crow flies; the jade hare runs. In the space of a single kṣaṇa, the new replaces the old. Where the first yang returns, the whole body penetrates through.
The flowering of the lamp-post is still steep and imposing. Roasting chestnuts, boiling yams—this is the livelihood of the patch-robed monk, practiced according to the season.
The rhythmic beat of the Hu family melodies is naturally clear; as the movement of the sun’s shadow shifts, where does it go? How lamentable this vast emptiness!"
In this vast world of dust, how few are those who tread the path of temporary rest? This year we see not the people of last year;
how many of the present generation have become ancient tombs? Zhang San and Li Si are drunk and muddled; they bring laughter to the staff of Gānlù.

Ascending the hall, he said: "I urge you all, one and all: recognize the Mind-King and all matters are finished. Picked up from amidst the heap of the six sense-objects, it has never been lost throughout kalpas.
The Master said: "How great and small [in stature] was the Great Being (Mahāsattva) Fu! He has lost it. Why?"
"Once you have been the great ocean, do not boast of your waters; were it not for Liangyuan, all would be but villages.
Entering the hall, he said: "Śākyamuni’s silence in his room was an offense as vast as the heavens; Vimalakīrti’s refusal to speak could not save himself.
How is this? How is this? His mouth is simply too small!"
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the matter beneath the patched robe? The Master said, "The heavens are parched; I grieve for the people. A monk asked, "What is Chan?
The Master said, "A single gust of foreign wind creates a mechanism in Han land. A monk asked, "'The six kinds of divine functions are empty or not empty;
the single round light is color or not color. What is this single round light? The Master said, "Brocade."
The scales do not emerge from the water. What is the sixfold divine function? The Master said: "How could a spiritual bird nest in a common dwelling? Question: What is the guest within the host?
The Master said: "Night travel is not permitted; you must arrive by dawn. Question: What is the host within the guest? The Master said:
"Though Chang'an is pleasant, it is not as good as one's old home. Question: What is the guest within the guest? The Master said: [He remained silent].
"If a person lacks foresight, they will surely have immediate cause for anxiety. "What is the Lord of Lords? The Master said, "When it is time to sever, one severs immediately;
thus one does not invite disorder. The monk bowed. The Master held up his whisk and said, "Guest and host are clearly distinct," and then descended from his seat.

Ascending the hall, he said: "The nectar of immortality is what is constantly spoken by the Buddhas and the Patriarchs; it is their calling out to you. Their discourse on the profound and the marvelous is the path for you.
Their wielding of staffs and shouts is to settle or stir you. Their gathering in and letting go is to kill or give life to you.

Their alternating roles of host and guest is to challenge and interrogate you. Their taking the head to serve as the tail is to exercise adaptability for you. Their 'knocking the bones and beating the marrow' is..."
"Be attentive! Walk side by side with your arms linked; this is your harmony. Sprinkle water and remain free from affairs; this is your rest. Now tell me:
where does the nectar dwell for the sake of people? After a long silence, he said: "If you cut down the cassia tree in the moon, its pure light will surely increase all the more."

Ascending the hall, he said: "Transmitting the Dharma and passing on the mind—taking what is wrong and making it right. Standing in the snow and severing one's arm—following the heterodox and pursuing the evil.
How can a monk of true substance evaluate this? The Great Master Bodhidharma reveals one shoulder."
Ascending the hall, he struck his staff and said, "From the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past, they have spoken only this Dharma. He then descended from his seat. Ascending the hall again, he said:
"With every rain and every sun, the mountain osmanthus grows ever greener. It is the marrow of Śākyamuni and the eye of Maitreya.
For those countless ones on the road who are mired in the mud, I ask them: when will be the day of their return?"
Ascending the hall, he said: "The waters of the Yellow River emerge from Kunlun; one who seeks clarity sees only increasing obscurity.
If you wish to transcend the karma of the Avīci Hell, you must extinguish the Tathāgata’s True Dharma Wheel. He struck his staff and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he struck once with his staff and said: "Master Yunmen said, 'All the Buddhas of the myriad dust motes are all here.
Can you discern them all? Even if you could discern them—clearly and decisively—you would still be obstructed by this staff.
If you can further turn it around, then feel free to go to India in the morning and return to China in the evening."
If you have not yet attained mastery, burn incense before the hall and join your palms behind it; strike the meditation seat and descend from the platform. When ascending the hall, say:
"Like a tortoise hiding its six limbs, one merely withdraws the head in vain; like a rabbit dividing into three, one has not yet mastered the art of transformation.

There is a certain type who says, "When it is appropriate to act, one acts; when it is appropriate to stop, one stops. This is very much like having the vulgar air of the world not yet removed. Directly—!
Even if one possesses the subtle clarity of heaven that leaves no trace of its origin, and turns what was before into what comes after with sovereign power, I tell you:
do not exert effort. It is not like this at all. Ultimately, how is it? After a long silence, he said: "The springtime of ninety days has passed in an instant."
Three thousand swordsmen came forth spontaneously.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Bird tracks appear in the void; lanterns are revealed upon the water. To discern their true essence:
a jade person riding an iron ox. Therefore it is said: "If released, they are enjoyed along the way; if gathered back, the blade is concealed within the sleeve."
Neither grasping nor releasing; the nostrils and the head remain as they are, pointing downward.
Entering the hall, he said: "Empty clarity is spontaneous; it requires no exertion of mental power. If you practice according to this, you will surely enter the Avīci Hell.
It is a place beyond conceptual thought, difficult for the conscious mind to fathom. Although there is a slight difference, alas, when the form is crooked, the shadow is bent."
Little do they realize that there are commands, both unmanifested and already manifested, and koans, both resolved and unresolved.
When one encounters a monk with clear eyes, everyone must be called upon to pass judgment. After all, what is it? After a long silence, he said:
"The staff of Deshan may still be tolerable, but Linji’s shout strikes terror into the hearts of men."
Ascending the hall, he said: "When it is time to cut, cut; do not invite disorder. What more is there to ask? This is a case of double layers. He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall again, he cited a monk who asked Yunmen: "What is it like when the trees are stripped of their leaves? Yunmen replied: "The golden wind reveals its essence."
"O virtuous practitioners of dhyāna, do you understand? It is said: 'While walking, it does not hinder the swinging of one's arms; while seeking others, it does not hinder seeking oneself.
If the mountain before one still exists, then everywhere there is no wind to stir the waves.
When the cry of a wild goose is suddenly heard, all are within the nest of the sorrowful man."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate. (He strikes the ground with his staff and says: "Not even a single stroke is required.
"The Bodhisattvas of the present each now enter perfect illumination; to let them pass would be a grave error.
"Those who practice and study in the future must take care not to create trouble where there is none. There are some fellows who, upon hearing someone speak in this manner, immediately say: "All..."
Because of the *upādhyāya*, one truly does not realize that the king of geese selects milk; he has never been of the same class as the duck.
Entering the hall, he raised the case of the late Master Ruidu, who addressed the assembly, saying: "In the secluded forest, birds call; in the azure stream, fish leap. Clouds unfurl like scrolls;
the sound of the waterfall is mournful. Can you yet believe in all these myriad phenomena? I show you a way of entry."
"Is it so? If you can truly believe this, it will do no harm to investigate it further. The Master said, "It is indeed so;
yet it is much like Meng Jiangnü sending away her winter clothes. This is why I told you: 'In the solitary village, yellow leaves fall;
in the deep courtyard, osmanthus blooms. The man of ambition laments the shortness of the day; the sorrowful person knows the length of the night.'"
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "Since recognizing the path of Caoxi, one understands that birth and death are not mutually related. What is the path of Caoxi?
The Master said, "A double signpost every ten li, a single milestone every five li. The monk bowed; the Master said, "Have you recognized the beginning of the path yet?
Another asked, "What is 'the former illumination and the latter application'? The Master said, "The flowers must bloom through the night."

"Set forth! Do not wait for the morning breeze to blow. "How is it that the prior is function and the subsequent is illumination? The Master said: "Without one matter, it is difficult to grow one wisdom.
"How is it that illumination and function are simultaneous? The Master said: "The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip; the sweet melon is sweet from stem to end.
"How is it that illumination and function are not simultaneous? The Master said: "The left eye is half white; the right eye is half black."
Ascending the hall, he said: "From where does the wind come? From where does the rain arrive? Beneath the skin there is blood; upon the face there is a nose.
These are presented in their entirety, with no concealment at all. Even a monk with clear eyes must still have a sudden flash of realization. What of this sudden flash? For now, do not fall asleep!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Those who have realized the truth do not even perceive realization; how much less so for those who have not? Why is this?
It is not something realized by the measure of the non-sentient; only wisdom can realize it. Yet this realization by wisdom is neither a realization nor a non-realization.
There are some fellows who, hearing such talk, do not know where it lands and immediately say: 'The patch-robed monks are just like these lecturers,' and thus they cannot avoid following along."
His desires were perverse; he said to others, "My arms are long but my sleeves are short; my legs are thin but my straw sandals are wide.
He struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from it.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The clear smoke is thin and light; the warm sun lingers slowly. A hundred birds sing and the mountain valleys resound;
a thousand flowers smile and the bees and butterflies swarm. If you can realize this clearly, you will reach the Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara without moving a step, right upon the level ground."
Entering the ocean of Mañjuśrī’s wisdom, compassion and insight are fused, and both quiescence and function are embraced.

If one can directly act in this manner, then before the gate of the patch-robed monk (the Zen master), one may roughly manage to find composure and settle the matter. If it is not so, the mind will shift with circumstances and the will will drift with events.
Wasting one's time in vain may still be tolerable, but a life of lonely hardship brings even greater sorrow to the heart.
Entering the hall, he said: "Fallen flowers follow the flowing stream; Crying birds dwell amidst the deep clouds. Do not be surprised by so many contradictions;
With advancing years, my hearing and sight grow dim. Have you not seen? The old Chan monk of seven hundred years Tells people only this: 'East Gate, West Gate.'"
[The Master] entered through the south gate and the north gate. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Picking gold from sand—those who are not of my own kind cannot do it. Taking it up and using it immediately—such people are rarely encountered.

Have you not heard it said: 'Night travel is forbidden; one must arrive by dawn'? If one is a vinegar-worm, one does not know the taste of sourness; if one is a clear mirror, [it reflects all things].
To merely reflect upon oneself is nothing more than being a frog in a well; how could one know of the vast ocean? It is like a painting of a tiger that, though unfinished, is still superior to a dog.
For those who have once let go their hands at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, I simply ask: walk alone through the crimson heavens.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Yesterday morning there was a bustling clamor; this morning there is a bustling clamor. The Persian lost his white woolen cloth, yet Shi-de found iron coins.
Do you know this? You must understand that there will surely come a time when these are put to use."
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said, "You lot, you sleepyheads! Do you know that all of your eyes are right here in my hands?
After a long pause, he threw down the staff and said, "I return your eyes to you;
go ahead and wake up as you please."
Next, while presiding at the Nengren Zifu Chan Monastery in Luzhou, he ascended the hall.

A monk asked, "How was it before the Buddha appeared in the world? The Master said, "Not a hair's breadth, not a speck of dust. The monk pressed further, "And how was it after he appeared in the world?
The Master said, "Filling the ditches and blocking the valleys. The monk asked, "What is the difference between his appearing and not appearing? The Master said, [as before].
The Master said, "When people are level, they do not speak; when water is level, it does not flow.

The Master then continued, "Generally speaking, when one comes forward before the great assembly to proclaim this matter, one must be a monk of the fundamental division (*benfen*) for the seal and the box to fit together and for the occasion to be decisively resolved.
As soon as there is any ambiguity or error, there is immediately a separation."
How much more so when the pivot of the mechanism turns—the Buddha-eye itself remains bewildered; when the Patriarch’s command is put into action, how can ordinary sentiments fathom it?

Thus, beneath Deshan’s staff, those who know its weight find their orifices opened and all things pass through; within Linji’s shout, those who distinguish host from guest have their skin and flesh stripped away.
Like the King’s precious sword, who would dare meet its edge? Therefore it is said: "He who speaks loses the truth."
Those who know it revert to their original ignorance; those who possess it deviate from their true nature; and those who lack it bring harm to their very person.

Since the ailments are manifold, the remedies are likewise diverse in form. Unless one profoundly investigates the ultimate depths and directly reaches the fundamental source, how can water and milk be distinguished?

Being unable to distinguish between the refined and the coarse, one causes the vast and majestic power [of the mind] to undergo futile toil. Fundamental wisdom fails to arise, and the fault lies with the deluded consciousness.
One must clearly awaken to this; the principle is then manifest.

Ascending the hall, he said: "When one realizes that phenomena are not phenomena, then every phenomenon is True Suchness (*tathatā*). When one knows that the mind is not mind, then every moment of mind is profoundly still.

Where there is profound stillness, there is the constant application of wisdom as vast as the sands of the Ganges; where there is True Suchness, there is no interval between concealment and manifestation.
Since there is concealment and manifestation, how can there be no interval? After a long silence, he said: "Had I known earlier that the lamp was fire, the rice would have been cooked long ago."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of the Old Mother of East City. She was born at the same time as the Buddha and lived with him for an entire lifetime, yet she did not wish to see him.
Every time she saw the Buddha approaching, she would immediately turn away to avoid him; she moved about everywhere, up and down, but could nowhere escape him.

Finally, she covered her face with her hands, yet within the palms of her ten fingers, she saw the Buddha everywhere. The Master said: "The Elder Śākyamuni is of one and the same compassionate nature."
The skillful means of compassion are truly extraordinary. Even so, in the end, will you still attain it or not? Do you wish to understand?
Since there is no place to evade, join your palms and behold the Honored Countenance. One incense offering and one flame—how could paying such respect be difficult?
It is not difficult at all; look for yourself within the Hall of the Empty King.
Ascending the hall, he said: "Mind, mind, mind. Buddha, Buddha, Buddha. Mind-Buddha, Buddha-Mind. Mind, mind, Buddha, Buddha.
Mind and Buddha are non-dual. Yet you must further know that there is a single opening beyond this. What is this opening beyond?
He then said: South Jambudvīpa; North Uttarakuru."
Ascending the hall, he said: "The mani jewel is in the palm; it divides its radiance according to the five colors.
The precious moon is in the sky; it casts its reflection across the thousand rivers. Do you understand? [He strikes once with the staff. Misfortune does not enter the door of a cautious household."
Ascending the hall, he said: "To see seeing, one must be taught to penetrate the crown-gate. Where the crown-gate opens, the precious light divides.
It shines through past and present beyond compare; all Buddhas and Patriarchs of yore are but its descendants. Why is this so? In the end, the pearl rests within the water."
"One cannot avoid the thread because of the needle.
He ascended the hall and said: "The true does not conceal the false; it is like dozing with one's eyes open. The crooked does not hide the straight; there is still a slight difference.
Whether they be fish-eyes or bright pearls, they are all entirely up to you. If you intend to propose anything further, I dare not grant my approval."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: A high-ranking general from Jingnan sent an offering to Yunju and asked Master Ying, “The Tathāgata has a secret teaching, which Kāśyapa did not conceal.
I do not know what its meaning is. Ying called out, “Minister! The Minister responded, “Yes?

The Dharma-Dharma illuminates the mind; in every speck of dust, he extends his hand. Directly emerging from Huangmei, he manifests alongside Niushou. Lofty are the Twin Peaks;
as vast as heaven and enduring as earth.

Praising the Fifth Patriarch’s turning about at Zhugang: the method of the "Broken Head Seal" has its five petals in full fragrance, while a thousand disciples tread upon it. Whether one is outstanding or capable—who departs and who joins?
Who is separate and who is united?
I extol the Sixth Patriarch, who mounted the white ox-cart and received the seal of Huangmei; his essence vanished into the spirit, and he manifested swift power upon meeting the occasion.

His true track was without error, and the realm of Kun (the earth) attained great harmony. The robe ceased its transmission, for the Dharma is to be trusted only within oneself. A single drop from the Cao source rises to become a surging tide; the thousand...
Who alone has sustained the Ancient Southern School?
In praise of Master Lingyuan, two verses: A somersault beneath the fist;
advancing further on the tip of the pole. All rivers flow back to the same source; Lingyuan alone is revealed. Even shards and pebbles radiate brilliance.
Wind and clouds spread abroad; who could know them with a thousand eyes? The myriad minds cross over by themselves;
the numinous spirit resides in the source. Radiant yet silent, it is neither "you" nor "someone else. Running south and rushing north, they are equally Buddha and equally Mara.
The Buddha and the demon are both delusions; they are the calamity of the patch-robed monk, the thief of partial views.
Limping and dragging along—my teacher has no teacher. Muddled and amorphous—people recognize it yet do not know it. Thirty years ago, I smashed through a single fist;
even until now, empty space is completely filled.
Master Qin of Taiping possessed a throat of iron and stone;
beneath the White Cloud Mountains, he swallowed the thorny *liji* fruit. With the winds and frost as his commands, he displayed the *vajra* circle before the Wanzhu Terrace.
For ten years he presided over the monastic seat, his reputation resounding throughout the four seas. There was no Buddha... [he surpassed him].

The Dharma can be explained; there are public cases that must be put into practice. Why so much talk based on mere rumors? Advancing one step and retreating another—bowing in praise, I incur offense after offense.
The Master himself composed this true eulogy:
"The skin is so thick that the awl cannot pierce it; it is far too stubborn. Having not a single coin myself, I travel to various places to trade, from the fields of Huai to the lands of Shenzhou."
Repaying old debts, the hundred skeletal members crumble and disperse;
amidst this mediocrity, who can truly know the one eternal spirit? The silver moon does not fall into the clear river;
sitting facing the yellow chrysanthemums, autumn has already deepened.
Behold the film in the mirror with urgency; do not grasp the lantern-balls at the bottom of the water.
To transcend words, one must discern the timing of this moment—gaze upon the solitary eagle across ten thousand li of clear autumn.
On the shores of the South Sea, a rabbit grows two horns; atop Mount Mufu, the terrain is rugged and stony. Having wandered there for ten years, my heels have become cracked and peeling.
What point of spiritual acuity could I possibly seek? Seven errors, eight mistakes.
The iron ox rushes into the Jade Phoenix ranks; peerless since antiquity, now matched as one. Its entire being is majestically revealed to you;
having eyes but no mouth, how can you understand?
Once wearing a flower crown, he entered Eastern Lu; again carrying a staff with a horn, he reached Western Qian.
He detested Huangbo for having "not many seeds," yet he laughed and granted Shaoyang his profuse Chan.
Verses on Tending Cattle:

To the assembly, I show that in daily life one must tend the ox; let not the nose-rope leave your hand. An open field is not a place of spontaneity; taming and mastery depend upon the passage of days.
Since the whip and reins are of no further use, what remains of man and ox? At this moment, it is known only by oneself; only then does one awaken to the faults of the past.

One reads the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)—who would say that after the "Plucking of the Flower," the succession of the fragrant blossoms has continued directly to the present? In the end, the pearl contains water; it cannot be avoided that the thread depends on the needle.

The butterfly remains where the flower still is; as spring deepens, the grass grows deep as well. Leaning against the open expanse of the windowed chamber, I idly listen to the dragon’s roar from within the cave.
The Elder Jomok sent me this verse on the whisk, which speaks of "using this very thing" and "being apart from this very thing":
A single arrow leaves the string and falls into the shout; The red heart is struck within the red heart.
I have unleashed my great capacity for function in Jiangxi; you should take it up to revitalize the ancestral wind. Bear this burden without dreading its weight of a thousand *jin*.
Forge the sages and melt the common folk, skillfully releasing and gathering. This realization shall surely not be shared with those of other quarters.

Harmony lies within this very function, yet apart from this very function. Before the arrow leaves the string, it has already struck its mark; at the edge of a ten-thousand-fathom cliff, one lets go of the hand and returns home.

A single phrase of profound mechanism is the function of non-function; at this moment, the needle and the magnet are scrutinized and found to be without discrepancy. How could the debt of gratitude be anything less than a mountain or a hill?
Weighty! Vowing to sacrifice one’s life is as bold as a fine thread hanging from a mountain peak; following the waves, it is shared for a while with humans and devas.
The Inscription on the Complete Pointing of Master Kazan, the Layman Koran:
"Pointing" is precisely non-pointing. When responding to conditions, what conditions are there? This hut contains the entire Dharma-realm; in this very place, one returns to the profound truth.
Quiescence is neither function nor substance; arising is neither Buddha nor non-Buddha. Cease further questioning toward the South; a single smile opens up the subtle and the profound.
Minister Liu Ren has recently requested a Dharma name, to which I bestowed "Wutong" (Miao-tong).
Now having received your fine verse, I have composed this in response.

Phenomenon after phenomenon reveals the perfect wondrousness; mind after mind communicates only with itself. Lofty and distinct, they differentiate the fundamental from the manifest; vast and open, they transcend both extremes and the mean. When this is clearly realized, names are established;
when one dwells in peace, reality is that which is followed. How great is the state of non-action! Pei Yun possesses a solitary wind of integrity.
He immediately came forward and spoke in harmony, answering:

"When serving as an attendant, one is utterly detached from sense-bases and objects; only then does one recognize that objects are but dust. To realize there is nothing to be attained is the true attainment.
Magnificent and alone, the original light is revealed; whether one goes south or north, it is always thus."
When heaven and earth are shattered, the channel is none other than I; when the universe is wrapped and covered, I am not that channel. That channel and this "I"—who could recognize them?
When the essence is realized as profoundly mysterious, it simply remains as it is.
Lost in the making and unmaking of vast kalpas, today is not new and yesterday is not old.
By momentarily turning the light back for a fleeting instant, one suddenly perceives the Eternal Spirit and attains liberation.
In response to Master Miaoling’s composition on thanking for the Dharma-name “Knocking upon Oneself to Realize the Clarity Beyond Subtlety”:
When you first examine the source, you see no "lively" spirit; Where there is subtle liveliness, who can examine or knock?
With a sudden turn of the wheel of mechanism, awakening comes in solitary clarity.
The Layman Lingran offered a curved-wood meditation seat. Because he sat upon it for a small-scale public teaching (*xiaocan*), he showed the assembly with a verse:
"The family secret of Layman Lingran, this curved-wood seat, I vow to offer it for the Longling to sit upon throughout the eight directions.
A Zen student, alert and mindful, overturns it; Suddenly, the original radiance is revealed alone. As the original radiance penetrates through, he laughs 'he-he'; Boundless space presents itself."
A Single Aperture. A Persian from the South Sea plays the lute; every note he strikes is rendered in the melody of the Shanyu.
These four short verses are sent to the practitioner Xinran to provide a means for his contemplative appreciation, so as to advance him toward the refined and profound essence within this realm.
The mind is thus, and phenomena are thus; phenomena differ, and the mind differs. Through this coming from such difference, I grant you a handle—a fine handle within this.
You must have a flash of realization beneath these words; in profound stillness, one must remain alert. Skillfully play at the opportune moment.

The mind thus accords with the dharma; dharma after dharma passes away. Only when the Great Function is fully manifested does it truly penetrate the arising of all things. Each is distinct yet mutually inclusive; they do not conflict, for they grant one another’s existence.
If they do not conflict, how could they be otherwise? The Dharma-realm is but a single dwelling; within it, all is utterly real. Beyond this, everything is entirely empty and void.
Entrusting this to Master Xuli:

To clearly understand that gain and loss have nothing to do with me, you must reach the state where body and mind are transparently penetrating. When penetration occurs, forget conditions and conditions themselves become transparent.
From this point on, whether entering or departing, simply act as the occasion requires.
Traces remain within the worldly path, yet the mind is perfectly clear; only when both are fully realized does one manifest as a true man of honor.
When the eight winds enter entirely into the realm of Vairocana, what need is there to laboriously ask the Patriarch for secret instructions?
Seeing Off Master Won on His Return to Longshan To attend upon the Elder Saramok (Jomok), I have never seen my teacher ill.
You go now to personally inquire after the health of our teacher; you and I are fellow disciples, there is no different path between us.
Though we do not follow one another step by step, who would say that traveling the long road is without a companion? It is precisely appropriate to maintain mindfulness at every moment.
I am here. I feel ashamed that I have failed to fulfill my responsibilities and remain confined to a narrow scope; though my mind dwells in silent contemplation, my body remains far removed.

That you could so urgently prioritize righteousness over personal convenience and go forth with both body and mind—by whom else could this have been accomplished? Though the Dragon Mountain lies a thousand li away, it will not take long to reach.

I fear that even my returning heart may find the flight of the monk’s staff too slow. Serving the Master who is ill as if he were oneself, and regarding one who is not a relative as a true kinsman—this is the true support for the path. Double Creek.
Mount Mufu is not far away; every going and every coming is a wondrous appointment.
I see you off, Chan Head Seat, as you return to Yongjia.
A single phrase penetrates all myriad transformations. For twelve years now, he has had no mouth. As he departs from me, he points distantly toward the sea mountains.
Returning, the Geese-Avalanche Peak lets out a lion’s roar; this principle is manifest and not concealed. With a mind hidden in tranquility, one enjoys a light that is more than sufficient.
A single drop from the Cao River flows through the ages; the sublime legacy of ancient awakening shakes the Great Tang.
If anyone asks about the family style of face-to-face encounter: to catch fish, one must be Xie Sanlang.
Sent off attendant Cí to attend to his parents at the place where his worldly ties were severed;
he studies our Way while his filial piety and righteousness remain firm as he thinks of his mother leaning on her gate.
To achieve a single blow that serves both purposes, he takes leave of me to return home and inquire after their well-being.
Seeing off a Monk Returning to Yongjia:
Everywhere he constantly attends upon One-Night Awakening; His true karmic affinity was not in Yongjia. Returning me back this very day, he goes his way;
The great trichiliocosm is all but a flower in the eye.
In the style of Hanshan. Four stanzas. What thing is this?
It circulates everywhere, leaking forth the wondrous mechanism. When spring is clear, the mountain birds sing; at the close of day, the cave clouds return.

Pointing at the finger, one asks if it is the horse; the mind is neither Buddha nor non-Buddha. Who can identify with both? Hand in hand, we enter the profound mystery. In a single thought, one penetrates the limit of reality;
in every speck of dust, the secret treasury opens. Who is the master standing before us? Letting go of all, one becomes their own matchmaker.
The great ocean is gathered within a single pore; the divine pearl is hidden within the oyster’s womb. At such a time, one knows that the Buddhas and Patriarchs have still come from the outside.

When inquiring of the Patriarch who came from the West, is the human mind existent or non-existent? How can one point directly downward? Morning and evening, how does one transform the ordinary person?
The Luo River is as clear as a silken ribbon; Mount Song is as magnificent as a painted scroll. Those who do not know the ultimate reality stubbornly claim there are differences.

To see the Way is to cultivate the Way; with no-mind, who would fail to awaken to the mind? There is neither ordinary nor sage; creation and destruction have existed thus from ancient times until now.
Green cascades flow with fallen leaves; a gentle breeze enters the still forest. Who comes beneath the rocky crag to teach you how to thread the needle at night?

*Three Poems on Dwelling in the Mountains* After all, dwelling in the mountains is best for a monk. In a stone chamber or thatched hut, one nurtures the sickly body. Opening one's eyes, one does not know whether the light belongs to—
Day after day, turning my head, I see only the shadow following the person. In secret communion, snakes and tigers are true friends; laughing, I meet with birds and fish through our original cause.
When a guest asks how long I have dwelt in the mountains, I reply: "With every fresh herb comes another spring."
A solitary monkey and a gaunt crane gaze coldly at one another; with a hundred patches and three robes, they endure the year’s chill. One does not intend to seek another Buddha with the mind;
it was once by parting the weeds that the hidden orchid was seen. Who calls out in the empty valley and can respond? I allow myself to play the silent lute in secret.
If you say there is originally not a single thing, know that you have been personally deceived by the Patriarch.
Facing the window, there are only fine rivers and mountains; at year’s end, no one comes or goes with me. I idly watch white clouds arise from the emerald peaks;
in stillness, I hear the clear sounding-stone fall amidst the murmuring stream. It is easy to distinguish sound entering sound, yet difficult to perceive emptiness hidden within emptiness.
If this state cannot be gathered and held, it will simply follow the flowing water down into the human world.

The old fisherman, with white hair too weary to comb, has no worries for a hundred things. With the sea gulls, he drifts idly day after day. How many times have honors and insults come and gone in this clear dawn?
Before my eyes, a single leaf-boat upon the misty waves. After the rain falls over Lake Dongting, he sings under the moon as he rows; when the frost flies over Yunmeng, he is drunk.

Autumn eyes; a raincoat and line, the late sun slanting on the reeds by the shore. Leisurely tapping the golden needle to fashion a fishing hook, the cowherd boys call out to one another with rustic songs.
Letting the oxen loose at the ancient ferryhead, when a traveler asks for the way, he simply does not respond.
Looking back, I smile as I let my light reed float upon a solitary boat.
Five Poems Written Incidentally in the Mountains:
The myriad transformations have never been interrupted; the true mechanism is naturally wondrous. White clouds swirl to form a canopy; green ridges stand in rows like screens.
The fierce tiger roars in the cold valley; crows and ravens clamor at the evening glow. The Gate of Perfect Penetration stands wide open—why do you not all return together?
Sitting upon the rock, I lament my solitary reflection; gazing at the clouds, I laugh at this body of mine. The boundless meaning of the meditation cushion—to whom shall it be entrusted?
Growing old, I have become secluded and remote; even the meaning of the Westward Transmission is lost to me. I do not know if the lion’s roar is like the cry of a wild ape.
Delighting in the crisp, clear scenery, I linger as I leave my thatched hut. One encounter with Hanshan under the moon—like a bright moon sealing upon a cold pool.
By the crag’s edge, spring is nearly spent. (Four stanzas:
By the crag’s edge, spring is nearly spent. Fragrant breezes arise, pervading the earth; my bag holds a bottomless bowl. Reclining high, I laugh at the city of Vaiśālī.
By the cragside, spring is nearly spent; The remaining flowers naturally dot the moss. A traveler beneath Mount Niutou Once beheld the arrival of the Patriarch.
By the cragside, spring is nearly spent; Before the steps, the green grass grows deep. Liu Yang possessed such noble character— In a single phrase, there was one who understood.
By the mountain crags, spring is nearly spent; my foolishness and delusion grow ever more intense. From time to time I encounter a rustic elder, and together we chant "Ling-lan-la.

On the eve of the year, we secretly carry one another through the passing scenes in a state of complacency; who could have thought that forgetting everything together is the essential ford? Not a hair’s breadth has moved, yet people are lost to themselves.
Old man, look! The crying birds announce the fragrant spring.
A monk asked about the meaning of the six characteristics; in response, he showed him this verse:
"The fire-star in the heavens runs upon the earth; The clay ox steps on it and burns his mouth. The donkey suffers the pain, while the horse-man..."
In his anger, he struck down thirty or fifty bushels of *yangmei* fruit.

Beholding the Twin Pagodas, they vied with one another in transmitting the "Hanging Hand" and the three barriers; again, it was said that he displayed a single fist to face the enemy. Who would believe that from the roots of the clouds, a pair [of pagodas] surged forth?
The pagoda stands; the pines and winds are distinct, even more profound and mysterious.

Striving toward my initial resolve, the four mountains press in from all sides with a force like a rushing torrent. If the three rats gnaw at the creeping vines, how can they endure for long? Do not rely on your youth to treat the white-haired old age with contempt.
Day by day, you must urgently turn back your head and enter the Gate of Emptiness.

You are a monk traveling through all quarters to propagate the Dharma, acting without contrivance; yet you do not even sit in non-action. The red dust of the world is inherently still— who needs to untangle its confusion?

Though the single trigger is subtle and constant, it must be like a crossbow capable of pulling a thousand-jin weight. When the crossbow is fully drawn and the trigger is released, the target is pierced with effortless ease.

To enter the red dust of the mundane world while maintaining this state is called "the eye within the dust. Responding to changes as they arise remains in suchness; thus, one skillfully guides others without any deliberate effort.

Who determines poverty or wealth? A true friend is found wherever one encounters them. When you have attained your heart's desire, return home early; this will provide me with an inexhaustible treasury.
Who cares if the rivers and roads are frozen and not yet open? Smiling, I carry my iron bowl out of the mountains. The flower of the mind does not fall into the hands of the Eastern Lord (Spring);
I shall wait to plant the sacred root within the fire.
Who in the world knows that lotuses grow from within fire? To enter the marketplace, one must be a true man. When the old fellow of Vaiśālī struck the key note, he reported:
"In recent years, my eyes have been covered with rheum."
The ambrosial bowl has no bottom; Zen practitioners must pick it up and examine it. Amidst the vast expanse of dust and soil, there is one Buddha and two Bodhisattvas.
Upon encountering the old Vimalakīrti, they gently converse with him: "The donor is not the field of merit—who is it that incurs defeat?"

Eh! Original enlightenment is fundamentally luminous; by riding upon conditions, one must realize its wondrous essence. Standing like a sheer cliff, who can be its peer? Through skillful means (*upāya*), laughter arises.

Myriad transformations are the full functioning of the mechanism; a thousand mechanisms are complete within a single illumination. When the waves darken it, does the moon ever perish? When the water is clear, the light shines of itself.

Having realized emptiness beneath the forest trees, one must accomplish tasks amidst the dust of the world; as tasks unfold, one realizes true emptiness, and from within that emptiness, one expands the work of transformation.

Within the state where phenomena are empty and emptiness itself is a phenomenon, one refines and melts the mind into a precious vessel. When this precious vessel is filled with the essence of *amṛta*, it is called the flavor of nectar.
How does the gift of food compare to the gift of Dharma? Green willows and young grasses through many springs. Holding your bowl well, go among the marketplace;
do not spare your eyebrows when pointing them out to others.

Motto: To perceive change is delusion; for consciousness to be serene is awakening. Action and cessation are mutually dependent; birth and death are intertwined. How wondrous is this spiritual penetration!

Indistinctly, it is fundamentally simple; its function is equal to its nature. Speech and silence are both manifestations; the three periods of time appear before one, and the ten directions respond instantaneously.
It knows without knowing, and dwells without dwelling. Contemplating this great vision forever, one takes the mind alone as the primary task.
The Inscription for the Zhi Hall.
The layman Zi-yuan of Taiyuan named his hall "Zhi" (Rest), intending to seek the peace of self-attainment. He said to the rustic Changling:
"The 'rest' of my dwelling hall is not the 'rest' of halting a flow. If one were to use 'rest' to stop a flow," [it would be a mere suppression].
This stillness is also a flow. When there is a place where one stops, one remains ignorant of the profound source; all such states do not transcend the realm of form and dependency.
What is now called "stopping" is the stopping of contemplation (*guan*). When stopping and contemplation coexist, one forgets stopping.
In this forgetting of stopping, whether speaking or remaining silent, moving or still, everything is nothing other than stopping. This is precisely how one achieves true stopping. — Changling Ye.

A person replied to him, saying: "As for the subtlety of the Way, these words have captured it. If one must certainly seek a means to realize and verify it as it truly is, there is nothing that could surpass this.
Thereupon, he composed an inscription for it, which says:
How profound is this hall! It is the complete contemplation and the complete cessation. This cessation is itself the cessation; how could its manifestations ever come to an end?

Such is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). To fail to remain silent is a sickness; it is only by returning to this state that one finds rest. Profound silence gives rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*); when wondrous concentration reaches its perfection, the essence of the mind emits light.
Without stepping outside the door or window, one clearly perceives the ten directions. Having transcended both movement and stillness, there remains nothing that dwells.
Abiding therein with peace, one encounters the source at every turn.
The Recorded Sayings and Biography of Master Changling Zhuo of Tiantong Wanshou Chan Monastery in Tokyo.
The Master’s name was Shouzhuo. He was born into the Zhuang clan and was a native of Quannan. In his early twenties, he traveled to the capital to pursue his studies at Tian... [Monastery].
At Qing Temple, he underwent the examination on the Mahāyāna Sūtras and received ordination. He traveled to study in Sanqu, where he met Chan Master Nanchan Qingya.
One day, he presented his realizations to Qingya, who immediately certified them. The Master felt confident in his own mind and departed.

Arriving at Dinghui in Gusu, he followed Chan Master Zunshe to master the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, eventually reaching its profound depths. Zunshe held him in high esteem and treated him with special respect. At that time, Ling...

Chan Master Yuanqing resided at Taiping in Longshu, where his reputation for the Way resounded throughout the four quarters. [The author] therefore went to rely upon him. Upon his initial arrival, he attended the night assembly;
it happened to strike home his own spiritual ailment, and he was suddenly awakened, thinking, "This is truly my teacher. He surrendered himself with sincerity and entered the inner chamber.
Lingyuan opened the great furnace and bellows for him, forging him with various skillful means and wisdoms. The Master responded to each challenge without fail, and furthermore, he was cautioned...

He maintained a profound silence and never sought self-promotion; the Master understood his intent. He remained submerged among the masses, never wavering in his integrity and never seeking intimacy for its own sake.
No one recognized him, and all considered him headstrong. When Lingyuan moved to Huanglong, the Master attended him there for ten years.
One day he took his leave. Lingyuan sent him off with a verse, the first few characters of which read: "Dwelling without dual intent, acting with total sincerity;
thus one transcends the City of Transformation to ascend the Precious Abode. Yet, with his tongue tucked in and his mind in profound stillness, he did not engage in talkative brilliance.
Therefore, wherever he went, few people knew of him. I alone observed that he lacked the petty peddlers and short-sighted schemers found among the scholars of the present age.
The Master’s concern was that he could traverse the long journey by walking, yet he wished to apply the whip; he sought to sever all subtle attachments for the sake of a hundred years.
These were all the Master’s actual records. Subsequently, he went to Taiping to visit Chan Master Fojian Qin, who invited him to occupy the position of First Seat.

The Master regarded Qin as a true知己 (zhiji—“one who knows himself”), so he did not firmly decline. The assembly was all filled with doubt and alarm, but when they heard his instructions, there was none among them who did not feel profound admiration and submission.
When Governor Sun (Jie) heard of his reputation, he happened to find the post of Director of the Ganlu Monastery vacant and invited the Master to preside over it.

The Master’s diligent colleagues and the assembly all wished him not to go, saying, "This is a desolate village and a ruined monastery; we fear you will have no success there. The Master replied, "I do not worry about such things;
I simply consider what lies within myself. He set off with his satchel slung over his shoulder, and the monks followed him, each contributing their own provisions and belongings.

He expanded and renovated the halls and chambers. Although the common people had long been known as difficult to transform, by this time they were all unanimously inclined toward faith and took pleasure in not becoming weary;
in the end, the weeds and brush were transformed into a precious monastery (*ratnagṛha*). Someone asked: "By what path did he bring about the transformation of such stubborn and fierce people?"
He said, "How could I have the leisure to go from house to house and door to door to transform them? However, as descendants of our Buddhas and Patriarchs, we simply do not lack for our task;
it is that they do not know why it is so, yet it is so. Some praised and marveled at the uniqueness of his words.
After the opening of the hall, Lingyuan saw the letter and said, "My responsibility may now be entrusted [to you], and the tradition of Jicui may be pursued.
He then took up his whisk as a token of the Dharma-pledge and presented this verse: "Using this very thing, yet detached from using it;
A single arrow leaves the bowstring and falls amidst the shouts. The red heart within the heart pierces the red heart; It awakens my great functional power of Jiangxi. [He] bestowed [the whisk].

"You ought to revitalize the ancestral style; carry this burden without shrinking from its weight of a thousand *jin*. Forging the holy and melting away the mundane, you must be adept at both letting go and gathering in.

It is certain that your realization will not be shared with those of other quarters. He further said: "Among those in the world who claim to be successors, many are famous in name but empty in reality."
At this time, it is natural that I cannot forget you; I place my hopes in you, and can you not likewise act according to what is natural and attend to my concerns?

Furthermore, it is said: "Grasp the pivot of responding with goodness and dwell in the essential point of harmonious penetration. In principle, one must follow antiquity; in practice, one values adaptation to the times.
To be indolent and rely on external conditions, or to stand alone and fulfill only one's own duties—these require self-exertion and do not wait for my words."
Furthermore, he successively moved to Zifu Temple in Luyang and Tianning Temple in the capital, both of which were places where the Dharma seat had long been abandoned.

Before long, however, these sites flourished once more like nectar. Throughout his life, he was diligent and frugal in his expenditures; in every residence, his meals consisted of barely enough rice for gruel.
He once said to the assembly: "Lingyuan entrusted me with this: I must undertake what others find difficult, and I shall counteract the trends of the times."
What he deemed urgent, I have worn upon my person for my entire life and dare not forget. Whenever he presided over a multitude, he invariably led them by his own example.

Without establishing formal rules or regulations, they were transformed through his discipline. His countenance was stern and cold; thus, people from all quarters gave him the nickname "Iron-Face Zhuo."
When he first moved to the Changling Hall at Taiping, the monastics began to refer to him as "Changling.
On the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month in the fifth year of the Xuanhua era, he ascended the hall and sang the "One Song of the Twelfth Month" of Yunmen.

Because he used this to fervently exhort and admonish his disciples, on the twenty-seventh day, he bid farewell to the assembly, sat peacefully, and passed away. He had lived for fifty-nine years and had been in the seat [of teaching] for... [years].
Thirty-two years after his passing, on the twenty-fifth day [of the first month], his body was cremated. Three items remained unburnt; the śarīra relics that fell were of five colors and translucent.
Those among the clergy and laity who obtained them were beyond counting. A stūpa was erected in the capital to the right of the stūpa of the Chan Master Fayun Yuantong.
This was on the twenty-first day of the first month in the sixth year [of the Shaoxing era]. The fourteenth year of Shaoxing, the first month.
The fifteenth day. Prepared respectfully by the disciple Jie Shen.
An appended note from the *Pudeng lu*, volume ten, concerning Chan Master Changling Shouzhuo (etcetera), dated the fifth year of the Xuanhua era.
On the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month, he suddenly manifested his passing into nirvana.

On the day of the cremation, the Emperor dispatched a palace messenger with incense, holding a golden tray to seek śarīra relics. As the incense was burned, something struck the tray with a metallic *keng* sound.

Upon inspection, several five-colored grains, each as large as a bean, were found within it. The messenger hurried back to the capital, where the Emperor beheld them with great joy, and the news spread throughout the city.
This is a magnificent occasion.
